title: What the Voice Is Saying
theme: Tone and attitude: reading the feeling behind the words
objectives: I can name the feeling or attitude behind a speaker's voice with a precise word.
I can use clues in a text to prove which tone word fits.
I can use the endings -ic, -ical, -ful, and -ent to understand describing words.
I can write a short description that makes a tone clear without naming the feeling too early.
rationale: Grade 7 opens with tone because every later skill, from judging a source to reading a poem, depends on hearing attitude as well as information. The ten words cover three areas: feelings about the past or the future (wistful, melancholy, apprehensive), how seriously a speaker treats a topic (solemn, earnest, whimsical, irreverent), and attitudes toward other people and events (indifferent, sarcastic, cynical). Students already know happy, sad, and mad; these words separate shades those labels blur, such as sad-and-longing versus sad-and-gloomy, or doubting versus mocking. Three words (cynical, irreverent, sarcastic) also show how a base word grows an adjective ending.

words.def: Feeling a quiet, gentle longing for something in the past or out of reach.
words.ex: The wistful old sailor stared at the harbor and remembered the ship he once commanded.
words.ex2: Her wistful smile showed how much she missed summers at her grandmother's farm.
words.nonExample: A person cheering about tomorrow's party is not wistful.

apps.academic: A poet may use a wistful tone to show that a happy time has ended.
apps.spoken: I felt a little wistful when I saw my old school.
apps.writing: Use wistful for a soft, sad longing, not for anger or fear.

cloze.s: The ___ look on the retired dancer's face showed how much she missed the stage.

cloze2.s: Gazing at the faded photo of his old street, Omar felt ___ and wished those days could return.

misuse.s: Mina's wistful voice was full of rage as she screamed at the referee.
misuse.why: Wistful describes a quiet, gentle longing, not screaming anger.

visual.alt: A person gazing out of a rain-streaked window.

words.frame: I feel wistful when I remember ___.

words.def: Worried or uneasy about something that may happen soon.
words.ex: Dana was apprehensive about the audition, so she rehearsed her song one more time.
words.ex2: The apprehensive passengers gripped their seats as the plane shook in the storm.
words.nonExample: Looking forward to a favorite ride is not being apprehensive.

apps.academic: Characters who are apprehensive often hesitate before a turning point in the plot.
apps.spoken: I'm a bit apprehensive about the test tomorrow.
apps.writing: Use apprehensive when a character worries about a future event, not one that already happened.

cloze.s: The ___ goalie bit her lip as the other team's best player lined up the penalty kick.

cloze2.s: Everyone in the waiting room looked ___ as they listened for the doctor to call a name.

misuse.s: Lucas felt apprehensive about the roller coaster because he was sure it would be the best ride of his life.
misuse.why: Apprehensive means worried about what may happen; expecting the best ride is the opposite.

visual.alt: A nervous face next to a tall roller coaster.

words.frame: I would feel apprehensive about ___ because ___.

words.def: Not interested or concerned; showing no care about what happens.
words.ex: The indifferent clerk kept scrolling on his phone while the customer waited.
words.ex2: Many voters feel indifferent about local elections, so few of them show up.
words.nonExample: A fan who cries when her team loses is not indifferent.

apps.academic: Historians ask whether a leader was cruel or simply indifferent to suffering.
apps.spoken: Honestly, I'm indifferent; pick whichever movie you like.
apps.writing: Use indifferent to show that a character feels nothing about an event that matters to others.

cloze.s: The ___ guard barely glanced at the tickets and waved the whole line through without caring who they were.

cloze2.s: Although the class begged for a decision, the ___ principal shrugged and said it made no difference to him.

misuse.s: She was indifferent to the contest, so she stayed up all night worrying about who would win.
misuse.why: Indifferent means not caring; worrying all night shows she cares a great deal.

visual.alt: A person shrugging while looking at a phone.

words.frame: A person who is indifferent about ___ might say ___.

words.def: Saying the opposite of what you mean in order to mock or poke fun.
words.ex: “Great catch,” said the sarcastic coach after the outfielder dropped the ball for the third time.
words.ex2: His sarcastic reply, “I just love waiting in line,” made the whole class laugh.
words.nonExample: A heartfelt thank-you that you really mean is not sarcastic.
words.rel: a tone that says the opposite

apps.academic: A sarcastic narrator says one thing so that readers will understand the reverse.
apps.spoken: I can tell you're being sarcastic, so I'll ask again seriously.
apps.writing: Use sarcastic when a character's words and true meaning are opposites.

cloze.s: When Jaya said, “Oh, wonderful, more homework,” her ___ tone showed she was not happy at all.

cloze2.s: The ___ remark that the broken umbrella was “perfect for this weather” made the soaked group groan.

misuse.s: The sarcastic speaker meant every word of her praise and said exactly what she felt.
misuse.why: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant, so meaning every word is not sarcastic.

visual.alt: A person rolling their eyes beside a speech bubble.

words.frame: A sarcastic comment about ___ might be ___.

words.def: Very serious and formal, not joking or playful.
words.ex: The judge gave a solemn nod before reading the verdict.
words.ex2: At the memorial, the crowd stood in solemn silence.
words.nonExample: A birthday party full of games and jokes is not a solemn event.

apps.academic: A solemn tone in a speech tells listeners that the topic is weighty.
apps.spoken: He made a solemn promise to keep the secret.
apps.writing: Use solemn for formal, serious moments such as ceremonies and vows.

cloze.s: The ___ ceremony began with a long silence, and no one so much as smiled.

cloze2.s: In a ___ voice, with no hint of a smile, the captain announced that the ship would not return to port.

misuse.s: The solemn announcer kept giggling and cracking jokes throughout the ceremony.
misuse.why: Solemn means serious and formal; giggling and joking are the opposite.

visual.alt: A balance scale beside a lit candle.

words.frame: A solemn moment is one when ___.

words.def: Serious and sincere, with real effort or deep feeling behind it.
words.ex: The earnest volunteer asked three questions before starting, because she wanted to do the job right.
words.ex2: In an earnest letter to the mayor, the students explained why the crosswalk needed a light.
words.nonExample: An apology tossed out with a laugh and a shrug is not earnest.

apps.academic: An earnest speaker usually backs up feelings with reasons and effort.
apps.spoken: She was so earnest about helping that everyone wanted to join her.
apps.writing: Use earnest for a character whose seriousness is real, not an act.

cloze.s: The ___ young intern stayed late every night and asked how she could improve.

cloze2.s: Looking her in the eye, Marcus made an ___ promise to practice every single day.

misuse.s: Her earnest apology was only a joke that she did not mean, and she laughed while saying it.
misuse.why: Earnest means seriously meant; a joke she does not mean is the opposite.

visual.alt: A student with a raised hand beside a handwritten note.

words.frame: An earnest person shows it by ___.

words.def: Playful and imaginative in an unusual, charming way.
words.ex: The whimsical garden had a teapot fountain and a gate shaped like a giant key.
words.ex2: Her whimsical poem described the moon wearing a hat made of clouds.
words.nonExample: A plain gray form with rules and boxes is not whimsical.

apps.academic: A whimsical illustration can make a serious idea easier to remember.
apps.spoken: That's a whimsical idea, and I love it.
apps.writing: Use whimsical for charming oddness; it is a positive word.

cloze.s: The ___ illustrator drew a fish riding a bicycle and a cat reading a map.

cloze2.s: Instead of a plain sign, the café owner chose a ___ one shaped like a smiling coffee cup.

misuse.s: Her whimsical plan was strict, ordinary, and exactly like every other plan in the office.
misuse.why: Whimsical means playful and unusual; strict and ordinary is the opposite.

words.frame: A whimsical idea for a ___ would be ___.

words.def: Doubting that people mean well; expecting selfish reasons behind what others do.
words.ex: The cynical reporter assumed the mayor's donation was only a way to win votes.
words.ex2: After hearing so many broken promises, Leo grew cynical about every campaign speech.
words.nonExample: Trusting that a stranger returned your wallet out of kindness is not cynical.

segs.m: a person who distrusts others' motives

apps.academic: A cynical narrator assumes that characters act only for their own benefit.
apps.spoken: Don't be so cynical; maybe they just wanted to help.
apps.writing: Use cynical for a sour doubt about motives, not for a calm, fair-minded check of facts.

cloze.s: The ___ shopper insisted that every “free gift” was a trick to get people to spend more money.

cloze2.s: Because she had been fooled before, Mei was ___ about the stranger's offer to help for nothing.

misuse.s: A cynical person trusts everyone and believes that every stranger has only good motives.
misuse.why: Cynical means expecting selfish motives, so trusting everyone is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person with narrowed eyes looking at a pile of money.

words.frame: A cynical person might say that ___ is only about ___.

words.def: Sad in a quiet, lasting way, often without one clear cause.
words.ex: The melancholy song about autumn made the whole room grow quiet.
words.ex2: A melancholy mood settled over the team after the last game of the season.
words.nonExample: The sudden anger of a lost argument is not melancholy.

apps.academic: Many poems about autumn have a melancholy tone.
apps.spoken: The rainy weekend left me feeling melancholy.
apps.writing: Use melancholy for a slow, thoughtful sadness that hangs around.

cloze.s: The ___ violin solo made the audience think about people and places they had lost.

cloze2.s: On the last day of summer, a ___ feeling crept over Nia as she packed her swimsuit away.

misuse.s: The melancholy children danced and shouted with joy at the surprise party.
misuse.why: Melancholy means quietly sad; dancing and shouting with joy are the opposite.

visual.alt: A violin resting beside a window streaked with rain.

words.frame: Music that sounds melancholy makes me think of ___.

words.def: Not showing respect for things most people treat as serious or important.
words.ex: The comedian's irreverent jokes about the school's strict rules made even the principal grin.
words.ex2: Irreverent humor can be funny, but it should not hurt people who are suffering.
words.nonExample: Bowing your head quietly during a national anthem is not irreverent.

morph.note: The final e of revere is dropped before -ent.

words.rel: making fun of what others honor

apps.academic: Satire often uses irreverent humor to question powerful people or old customs.
apps.spoken: That was an irreverent joke, but it did make me laugh.
apps.writing: Use irreverent for playful disrespect; decide whether you mean it as praise or criticism.

cloze.s: The ___ student drew a mustache on the portrait of the founder and laughed during the stern ceremony.

cloze2.s: His ___ attitude toward tradition annoyed the elders, who treated every custom as sacred.

misuse.s: She was irreverent toward the old flag, folding it with great care and bowing her head.
misuse.why: Irreverent means lacking respect; careful folding and a bowed head show deep respect.

visual.alt: A joker card lying on top of a golden crown.

words.frame: An irreverent joke about ___ could upset people who ___.

passage.title: The Last Show at the Maple Street Theater
paras: Ravi had one weekend to choose the voices for a radio show about the Maple Street Theater, which the town planned to tear down in June. Sorting the recordings was easy; deciding which clips to play was harder. “A person can say ‘it’s fine’ in six different ways,” his advisor, Ms. Duarte, warned him, “and each way means something different. Listen for the feeling underneath the words.”

The first clip came from Mr. Alvarez, who had taken tickets at the theater for forty years. His voice grew wistful whenever he described the velvet curtains, as though he were looking at them again. Next, a girl named Tala admitted that she felt apprehensive about the new community center because she could not picture anyone laughing in it. Ravi marked both clips with a star. Then he played a neighbor who answered every question with a shrug. “Tear it down, keep it, whatever,” she said. Her tone was indifferent, and no listener would learn anything from it.

The next speaker was harder to place. “Oh, sure, the council always listens to teenagers,” a man said, and Ravi heard sarcastic laughter in his voice. When the man added that nobody in town ever finished anything, the tone turned cynical, as if he expected every plan to be a trick. Ravi decided to keep a short piece of it, because a show made only of warm voices would not be honest.

Late in the afternoon he found three clips he had not expected. A retired actor told a story about forgetting his lines and was gloriously irreverent about the whole profession. A kindergartner called the theater “a cave where people keep their dreams,” a whimsical picture that made Ravi laugh out loud. Finally, the town historian read the names of the plays staged there in a solemn voice, and each title dropped like a stone.

By evening Ravi could build the show. He opened with Mr. Alvarez, closed with the historian, and placed Tala's earnest request for a small stage in the middle. The last recording was only a creaking floorboard and one note from the old piano. It left him feeling melancholy, a quiet sadness he could not quite explain, and he decided that was exactly the feeling the show should end on.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “wistful” most nearly describes a voice that is
choices: angry about what happened long ago
bored with the story it is telling
gently longing for something remembered
nervous about what will happen next
qs.why: Mr. Alvarez speaks as though he were looking at the curtains again, which shows a gentle longing for the past.

qs.q: Why does Ravi keep part of the cynical man's clip?
choices: He agrees that nothing in town ever gets finished.
He believes a show made only of warm voices would not be honest.
Ms. Duarte told him to include one angry speaker.
It is the shortest recording on the tape.
qs.why: The text states that a show made only of warm voices would not be honest, so the doubtful voice earns a place.

qs.q: The neighbor's answer, “Tear it down, keep it, whatever,” shows that she
choices: is deeply upset about the plan
is hiding her opinion behind a joke
is nervous about speaking on the radio
does not care which way the plan turns out
qs.why: She treats tearing down and keeping the theater as the same, which is what the narrator calls an indifferent tone.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Tala felt apprehensive about the new community center?
choices: She could not picture anyone laughing in it.
She marked her clip with a star.
She answered every question with a shrug.
She loved the velvet curtains.
qs.why: Apprehensive means worried about what may come, and Tala's worry is that the new place will be joyless.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The feeling in a voice can matter as much as the words it speaks.
Old theaters should never be torn down.
Radio shows should use only cheerful voices.
Teenagers make better interviewers than adults.
qs.why: Ravi's work, and Ms. Duarte's advice, center on listening for the feeling underneath the words.

write.prompt: Describe a voice you have heard, such as a coach, a relative, or a character in a show. Use at least three words from this unit to name its tone and prove it with a detail.

parts.m: relating to; having the quality of

study.task: Find the ending in wistful, sarcastic, cynical, and irreverent. Sort each word by its ending, say what the ending adds, and then write one sentence about a speaker who fits one of the words.

Write a sentence that uses both sarcastic and sincere to show how a speaker's words can differ from their meaning.

given: The poet read in a very serious voice.
The audience stayed quiet for a full minute.
combine.model: The poet read in such a solemn voice that the audience stayed quiet for a full minute.

given: The reporter doubted the mayor's gift.
She believed it was a trick for votes.
She had seen similar promises broken.
combine.model: Because she had seen similar promises broken, the cynical reporter believed the mayor's gift was only a trick for votes.

discuss: When is an irreverent joke harmless, and when does it cross a line? Use irreverent and one other word from the unit.
Is being cynical different from being careful about facts? Explain with cynical and earnest.
Which word in the unit best describes the mood of a rainy day, and why?
produce.explain: Explain how a speaker's tone can change the meaning of the words “That was a great idea.” Use sarcastic and one more word from the unit.

argue.prompt: Claim: A news report should always use a calm, neutral tone, even about sad events. Take a side and support it with two reasons that use words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A solemn tone would ___, while an indifferent tone would ___.

constructed.prompt: Two songs are both sad. One is about missing a happy past, and the other is about a long, heavy sadness with no clear cause. Use wistful and melancholy to describe each and explain how they differ.
look: matches wistful to longing for the past and melancholy to lingering sadness
explains the difference rather than treating the words as identical
constructed.model: The first song is wistful because the singer longs for summers that are gone. The second is melancholy because its slow, heavy sound makes the listener feel quietly sad even without a reason.

constructed.prompt: A classmate announces a plan to clean up the school garden. Write three short replies, one sarcastic, one earnest, and one cynical. Label each and explain which clue shows the tone.
look: writes three replies that really differ in tone
names a clue such as opposite meaning, real effort, or doubt about motives
constructed.model: Sarcastic: “Wow, because that will definitely fix everything.” The words mean the opposite of what the speaker thinks. Earnest: “I will bring gloves and stay until it is done.” The speaker offers real effort. Cynical: “They only want a photo for the newsletter.” The speaker doubts the motive.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten tone words, read a short narrative about choosing voices for a radio show, practice the adjective endings -ic, -ical, -ful, and -ent, and write about tone with evidence. The unit's habit is to name a feeling precisely and then prove it from a detail.

notes.va.wistful.adj: Wistful is gentle longing, not plain sadness. Ask students to separate sad-because-it-hurts from sad-because-it-is-over. Watch for confusion with wishful (hoping for a future thing).
notes.va.apprehensive.adj: Apprehensive points toward the future: worry about what may happen. Students often confuse it with apprehend (to catch). Keep the focus on the adjective and use a timeline to show future-facing worry.
notes.va.indifferent.adj: Indifferent is not caring which way something turns out; it is not the same as being different. Have students act out two shrugs, one bored and one calm, and discuss whether each is indifferent.
notes.va.sarcastic.adj: Sarcasm depends on a gap between words and meaning. Practice saying one sentence two ways. Some students, including some English learners, may miss sarcasm, so name the clue explicitly: exaggerated stress, an eye roll, or a context that contradicts the words.
notes.va.solemn.adj: Solemn is serious and formal, usually for important moments. Contrast with sad: a solemn voice is not necessarily unhappy. Use ceremonies as concrete examples.
notes.va.earnest.adj: Earnest is sincerity plus effort. Students may hear it as naive; show that an earnest person can also be smart. Connect to the grade 6 word sincere and ask what earnest adds.
notes.va.whimsical.adj: Whimsical is positive playfulness with an unusual twist. Contrast with silly (no charm) and with random. Ask students to design a whimsical object and explain what makes it unusual.
notes.va.cynical.adj: Cynical is doubt about motives, which is different from healthy skepticism (checking evidence). Use the cynical versus skeptical contrast carefully, since skeptical is a grade 6 word. Model the -al ending on the base cynic.
notes.va.melancholy.adj: Melancholy is quiet, lingering sadness, often with a thoughtful quality. The headword is also a noun; this unit teaches the adjective. Compare with wistful on a two-column chart: longing for something specific versus a general heaviness.
notes.va.irreverent.adj: Irreverent can be an insult or a compliment depending on the writer. Model the parts ir- + revere + -ent. Ask: irreverent toward whom, and does it hurt anyone? The aim is judgment, not a ban on humor.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “Mr. Alvarez slows down when he talks about the curtains. He is not angry and he is not afraid; he is longing for something that is gone. The word is wistful. Now the neighbor says ‘whatever’ about tearing the theater down. She does not care which way it goes, so indifferent fits. I can name each tone and point to the detail that proves it.”
discuss: Which of these words describe a speaker who might still be kind? Which usually do not?
How do you know a speaker is sarcastic if you can only read their words and cannot hear them?
misconceptions: Wistful and wishful mean the same thing.
Cynical is just a stronger word for skeptical.
Melancholy and wistful both mean plain sadness.
extend: Choose a poem or a scene from a class text and write a paragraph naming its tone with two words from the unit and a quoted detail.
Rewrite a three-sentence news report once in a solemn tone and once in an irreverent tone, then discuss which fits the topic.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit blunt, vague, reflective, and emphasize while discussing tone in the passage. Return to the tone words two days later with a quick sort by feeling, again at one week when analyzing any speaker or narrator, and again in unit 10 on narrators.

frames: I think the tone is ___ since the speaker says ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads one sentence aloud in a chosen tone without naming it. Partner B names the tone with a unit word and points to a clue in the voice or the words.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: nostálgico (wistful), aprensivo (apprehensive; may suggest fearfulness or hypochondria in some regions), serio y sincero (earnest), caprichoso (whimsical), desconfiado (cynical; cínico was avoided because it often means shameless).
Cognate flags for aprensivo and sarcástico should be confirmed.
Sense boundary: melancholy is taught only as an adjective; the headword is also a noun.
